source.title: Observation of Altered Iron Status Development During Noncompetitive Season Training in NCAA Division I Female Acrobatics and Tumbling Athletes

paper.citation: Pickler MC, Funderburk LK, Lee KM, Bolden LK, Chapman-Lopez TJ, Heileson JL, Gallucci AR. Observation of Altered Iron Status Development During Noncompetitive Season Training in NCAA Division I Female Acrobatics and Tumbling Athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2026. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000005584.
paper.abstract: This longitudinal observational study followed 29 NCAA Division I female acrobatics and tumbling athletes during a noncompetitive training period. Pre-post blood biomarkers and body composition were used to describe iron-status development in an understudied collegiate female sport.
paper.tldr: Serum ferritin declined across the training period while group hemoglobin and red-cell indices did not significantly change. The trend supports clinically governed surveillance in this population but does not identify a cause, establish anemia, or define a universal treatment threshold.
paper.methods: Blood biomarkers were assessed from October 1 to December 15, with DXA body-composition assessments in August and December. Serum ferritin, hemoglobin, red blood cell count and distribution width, total protein, estradiol, and progesterone were measured. Paired changes were tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and ferritin status was categorized using four previously published thresholds.
paper.findings: Serum ferritin decreased significantly, while red blood cell count, hemoglobin, and red-cell distribution width did not significantly change. Thirteen athletes, or 44%, were below 35 ng/mL before training compared with 79% after training. At the post-training assessment, one athlete exceeded 51 ng/mL and 96% were at or below 50 ng/mL.
paper.limitations: The study followed one team without a control group and did not measure dietary iron intake, detailed training exposure, menstrual history, supplementation adherence, inflammation, or other plausible contributors. Threshold classifications vary across clinical and sport contexts. Biomarker changes do not identify their cause, establish symptoms, or demonstrate that a specific intervention is required.
paper.practicalImplications: Use repeated iron-status assessment within an interdisciplinary clinical process for female collegiate athletes, especially when training exposure, symptoms, nutrition, or menstrual factors create concern. Interpret ferritin alongside hematology, symptoms, inflammation, diet, supplementation, and medical history rather than applying a single cutoff in isolation.
paper.athleteDev: Integrate nutrition education, recovery behaviors, symptom reporting, and clinically governed biomarker follow-up into the development environment. Avoid labeling an athlete's readiness or potential from ferritin alone.
paper.rtp: The study did not evaluate injury rehabilitation or return to sport. Iron-status findings may inform broader medical and readiness management, but they provide no clearance criterion or sport-participation restriction by themselves.
